title: Park Ridge to the Javits Center: the Methodist Girl, the Secretary's Million Miles, and the Ceiling That Held
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Methodist House at Park Ridge

stops.name: Chicago, birth at Edgewater Hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate harmonized between two lenses that disagreed by 790 metres of longitude, and locates the hospital site at 5700 N Ashland Ave only approximately
stops.campa: Hillary Diane Rodham is born on the north side of Chicago, first child of Hugh Rodham, a drapery-fabric jobber out of Scranton, and Dorothy Howell, who was raised by grandparents and strangers and left home at fourteen to keep house for a family that paid her three dollars a week. The rule that follows her out of this hospital is her father's: a Republican thrift that counts every light left burning. The Chicago birth certificate goes with her to Arkansas, to New York, and to the hundred and twelve countries she will cross as Secretary of State.
suggested_refs: Edgewater Hospital, 5700 N Ashland Avenue, Chicago, closed 2001
sources: Carl Bernstein, A Woman in Charge (2007)

stops.name: Park Ridge, the house on Wisner Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day default to 01. Coordinate is a Park Ridge town centroid, not the house: the published street number is disputed between 235 and 236 and the atlas states neither
stops.campa: The Rodhams move nine miles northwest to Park Ridge, a suburb of brick and elm where the fathers commute and the mothers do not. Dorothy sends her four-year-old daughter back out the front door to face a girl who has been hitting her, and tells her there is no room in this house for cowards. Hillary joins the Brownies, the Girl Scouts, the church youth group, and a neighborhood that runs entirely on organized activity. The corner of Elm and Wisner will one day carry the family name on a street sign, a few doors from where she learns to keep score.
stops.quote: I wasn't born a first lady or a senator. I wasn't born a Democrat.
stops.quote_source: Hillary Rodham Clinton, Living History (Simon & Schuster, 2003), opening lines. Only the first two sentences are quoted here: the widely circulated longer opening splices in sentences that do not adjoin these, as Open Library full-text search confirms
suggested_refs: Rodham Corner, at Elm and Wisner Streets, Park Ridge, Illinois

stops.name: Park Ridge, Maine Township High School East
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1961-1964 by Wikipedia; month set to the school year opening, day defaults to 01
stops.campa: She enters Maine East, wins her place in student government, and loses the race for student body president to a boy who tells her she is really stupid if she thinks a girl can be elected president. She debates, she edits, she is a National Merit finalist, she holds the vice presidency of her class. She writes to NASA to ask how a girl becomes an astronaut and receives an answer explaining that girls do not. Three years in, the township redraws its boundaries and moves her whole neighborhood out of this building.
suggested_refs: Maine Township High School East, 2601 W Dempster Street, Park Ridge

stops.name: Park Ridge, the University of Life at First United Methodist
stops.date_confidence: the King speech is attested to 1962 by the chronology lens; month and day are not fixed and default to 01. The pin is the church the van left from, not Orchestra Hall, for which the pool supplies no coordinate
stops.campa: Don Jones arrives from seminary as youth minister and starts what he calls the University of Life: Picasso prints, Salinger, Dostoevsky, and van rides into the Chicago the suburb was built to avoid. He takes his teenagers downtown to Orchestra Hall to hear Martin Luther King Jr. preach on remaining awake through a revolution, and afterward pushes the fifteen-year-old Republican forward to shake the preacher's hand. Two years later she works the phones for Barry Goldwater. She and Jones write letters to each other for the next forty years, and she keeps them.
suggested_refs: Orchestra Hall, 220 S Michigan Avenue, Chicago, site of the 1962 King address, unpinned in this file

stops.name: Park Ridge, Maine South and the first graduating class
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1965 for graduation; the June date is the ordinary commencement month and is not separately fixed in the pool
stops.campa: Maine South opens in 1964 with no seniors and no traditions, and she graduates in its first commencing class, in the top five percent, voted most likely to succeed. The school is younger than her high school career. Two teachers who went east recommend Wellesley, a college she has never seen, in a state she has never visited. She leaves Illinois a Goldwater Republican, with her father's ledger habits and her mother's instruction about cowards, and she is seventeen.
suggested_refs: Maine South High School, 1111 S Dee Road, Park Ridge, opened 1964

segments.name: Wellesley, Yale, and the Impeachment Room

stops.name: Wellesley College, the turn away from Goldwater
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1965-1969; the September date marks matriculation and is not separately fixed
stops.campa: She arrives at a women's college of a thousand students and is elected president of the Young Republicans in her first year. By her third she has resigned that office over civil rights, worked for Eugene McCarthy in the New Hampshire snow, and gone to Miami Beach with a group pushing Nelson Rockefeller against Richard Nixon. In 1968 she is elected president of the College Government Association. She majors in political science and writes her senior thesis on Saul Alinsky, who offers her a job organizing; she declines it for law school, and argues in the thesis that his method cannot scale.
suggested_refs: The Wellesley senior thesis on Saul Alinsky, restricted from public access 1993-2001

stops.name: Wellesley College, the first student commencement address
stops.date_confidence: attested; date supplied by the afterlife lens, coordinate retained at that lens's value rather than merged with the geography lens's, which differs by eight metres
stops.campa: The class petitions for a student speaker and the college, which has never had one in ninety-four years, agrees. Senator Edward Brooke speaks first, on patience and the dangers of coercive protest. The twenty-one-year-old who follows him sets her prepared text aside and answers him, in front of the trustees and the parents, on the subject of what the protests are actually about. Life magazine runs her photograph among the young voices of the year. She graduates with departmental honors in political science and leaves for Yale Law School in the autumn.
suggested_refs: Life magazine, 20 June 1969, on the class of 1969's student speakers

stops.name: Yale Law School, the library and the Child Study Center
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1969-1973; the September date marks matriculation and is not separately fixed
stops.campa: Yale takes twenty-seven women into a class of two hundred and thirty-five. She works at the Child Study Center on the law of children, edits the Yale Review of Law and Social Action, volunteers at New Haven Legal Services, and spends a summer with Marian Wright Edelman in Washington. In the library a student from Arkansas keeps looking at her; she walks the length of the room and tells him that if he is going to keep staring at her they had better know each other's names. Her article Children Under the Law argues that a child's legal incapacity is a policy choice and not a fact of nature.
suggested_refs: Hillary Rodham, 'Children Under the Law,' Harvard Educational Review 43 (1973)

stops.name: Washington, the Rayburn building and the impeachment inquiry
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The geography lens tags this posting [R] on a single source, Bernstein, and the chronology lens does not carry it at all; month and day default to 01
stops.campa: John Doar hires her onto the impeachment inquiry staff of the House Judiciary Committee, forty-four lawyers working the question of what a president can be removed for. She is twenty-six. She researches the grounds, listens to the tapes, drafts procedure. Nixon resigns on the ninth of August and the staff is dissolved with the work unfinished, and the young lawyers scatter into firms that will make them rich. She turns down the offers in New York and Washington and drives to Arkansas. Twenty-four years later this same committee votes articles against her husband.
suggested_refs: The House Judiciary Committee impeachment inquiry staff roster, 1974

stops.name: Fayetteville, the law school and the wedding in the living room
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage date; the faculty appointment is attested to August 1974
stops.campa: She takes a teaching post at the University of Arkansas School of Law, where Bill Clinton is already on the faculty and already running for Congress. She teaches criminal law, runs the legal aid clinic and the prison project, and turns him down twice. He buys the brick house on California Drive she once said she liked, and tells her he has bought it so now she has to marry him. They marry in its living room on the eleventh of October before a few dozen people, she keeps the name Rodham, and Arkansas notices that she keeps it.
suggested_refs: The Clinton House Museum, 930 W Clinton Drive, Fayetteville, the 1975 wedding house

stops.name: Little Rock, the Rose Law Firm
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1977; day defaults to 01
stops.campa: With her husband elected attorney general she joins the Rose Law Firm, older than the state bar itself, and works patent, intellectual property, and corporate defense. In 1979 she becomes its first woman partner. She co-founds Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families, chairs the board of the Legal Services Corporation in Washington, and takes a seat on the board of Walmart at Bentonville as its first woman member. The National Law Journal names her one of the hundred most influential lawyers in America. Her billing records from these years will be subpoenaed, declared lost, and found later on a table in the White House residence.
suggested_refs: The Rose Law Firm billing records, subpoenaed in the Whitewater investigation

stops.name: Little Rock, the Governor's Mansion on Center Street
stops.date_confidence: attested for the terms 1979-1981 and 1983-1992; coordinate corrected from the geography lens's value, which fell 1.4 km northwest near the Capitol grounds
stops.campa: She is thirty-one and First Lady of Arkansas, living in a Georgian house on Center Street, with a daughter born there the following February. She chairs the Rural Health Advisory Committee, then the Education Standards Committee that ties teacher testing to a sales tax increase and sends her into every county in the state to defend it. Voters turn her husband out after a single term, partly over her name. She becomes Hillary Rodham Clinton, he wins the office back in 1982, and he holds it for ten more years.
suggested_refs: The Arkansas Governor's Mansion, 1800 Center Street, Little Rock

stops.name: Little Rock, the Old State House on election night
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the steps of the Greek Revival building that served as the first capitol of Arkansas she stands beside her husband while he claims the presidency from George H. W. Bush, who conceded an hour earlier. In March she had answered a question about standing by her man by saying she was not some little woman standing by her man like Tammy Wynette, and had spent the spring apologizing for it. Buy one, get one free, he had told the crowds all year. She is forty-five and has never held an elected office.
suggested_refs: The Old State House Museum, 300 W Markham Street, Little Rock

stops.name: Washington, the West Wing office and the health care task force
stops.date_confidence: attested for the inauguration; the task force chairmanship is attested to January 1993
stops.campa: Five days after the inauguration the president names her chair of the Task Force on National Health Care Reform, and the office she takes is in the West Wing, not the East. Five hundred experts work behind a closed process and a lawsuit follows over whether a First Lady is a government employee at all. She testifies before five committees for hours without notes and is applauded for it. In September 1994 the bill dies without a floor vote in either chamber. In November the party loses fifty-four seats in the House, and the phrase Hillarycare enters the language as an insult.
suggested_refs: The Health Security Act of 1993, and the Association of American Physicians and Surgeons v. Clinton litigation

stops.name: Beijing, the Fourth World Conference on Women
stops.date_confidence: attested. Venue corrected from the geography lens, which pinned Huairou, fifty kilometres out, where the parallel nongovernmental forum met and where she spoke separately the following day
stops.campa: At the Beijing International Convention Center, before delegates from a hundred and eighty-nine countries and a government that has cut the broadcast feed, she lists the things done to women and refuses to call them anything but what they are. The State Department has asked her to soften the text and she has not softened it. The Chinese hosts have put the nongovernmental delegates fifty kilometres out at Huairou, in the rain, and she goes to them the next day too. The conference adopts the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action ten days later, on the fifteenth of September.
stops.quote: Human rights are women's rights and women's rights are human rights.
stops.quote_source: Remarks to the UN Fourth World Conference on Women, Beijing, 5 September 1995, in the abbreviated form carried by Wikiquote. The primary State Department transcript could not be fetched this session and the exact wording is therefore not established; the commonly cited fuller version ends 'once and for all'
suggested_refs: The Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, adopted 15 September 1995

stops.name: Tuzla, the airbase and the tarmac
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate and date both confirmed against CBS News footage of the visit
stops.campa: She flies into the airbase at Tuzla with her daughter, a comedian, and a singer, three months after Dayton, to see the American brigade wintering in Bosnia. There is a greeting ceremony on the tarmac and a girl who reads her a poem. Twelve years later, in a New Hampshire primary, she will describe running from the plane with her head down under sniper fire, and the network footage of the calm reception will run beside the claim for a week until she says she misspoke. Sinbad and Sheryl Crow, who were on the aircraft, remember no sniper fire either.
suggested_refs: CBS News footage of the arrival at Tuzla, 25 March 1996, rebroadcast March 2008

stops.name: Washington, the impeachment year in the residence
stops.date_confidence: attested for the House impeachment vote of 19 December 1998; the approval figure and the midterm result narrated here are general public record rather than pool-sourced
stops.campa: The House votes two articles of impeachment against her husband in December, eleven months after he told her, and the country, that there had been nothing with the intern. Her own approval stands near seventy percent, the highest figure of her life, and it is her husband's conduct that has produced it. She campaigns through the midterms and the party gains House seats, which no president's party in a sixth year had done since 1822. In the residence upstairs she is deciding whether to run for a Senate seat in a state where she has never lived.
suggested_refs: The Starr Report and the articles of impeachment adopted 19 December 1998

stops.name: Pindars Corners, the listening tour begins
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; county and coordinate corrected from the geography lens, which placed the hamlet in Otsego County forty kilometres away. Precision is hamlet-level, not farm-level
stops.campa: Daniel Patrick Moynihan, whose seat she means to take, brings her to his farm in Delaware County to begin what the staff calls a listening tour: no platform, no announcement, a hundred school gymnasiums and diners across sixty-two counties. He tells the reporters on the lawn that he thinks she will win and that she will be a great senator. She is still First Lady, still living in the White House, and no First Lady has ever run for anything. Most of the counties on this drive will vote for her twice and then, in 2016, vote for Donald Trump.
suggested_refs: Moynihan's farm at Pindars Corners, town of Davenport, Delaware County, New York

stops.name: Chappaqua, the house bought for a residency
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1999; month set to the reported closing period, day defaults to 01. Coordinate and label both corrected from the geography lens, which misplaced the hamlet by 2.2 km and called this the Rodham family home
stops.campa: They buy a white house on Old House Lane in Westchester County for one million seven hundred thousand dollars, and she registers to vote in New York. It is the first house the couple has owned since Fayetteville; for eighteen years they have lived in mansions the public provides and guards. The purchase is the answer to the carpetbagger charge and the charge sticks anyway, through a whole campaign. She wins the seat by twelve points against Rick Lazio, who crossed the debate stage during a question to put a pledge in front of her and demand she sign it.
suggested_refs: 15 Old House Lane, Chappaqua, New York, purchased 1999

stops.name: Washington, sworn in at the Capitol
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She is sworn in as the junior senator from New York seventeen days before her husband leaves the presidency, and for those seventeen days she is a sitting senator and the First Lady of the United States at once. Al Gore, defeated for the presidency five weeks earlier, administers the oath as president of the Senate. She takes the committee seats nobody wants, learns the courtesies, arrives early, and one at a time makes working allies of the Republicans who spent the nineties investigating her husband and her law firm.
suggested_refs: US Senate Historical Office records for the 107th Congress

stops.name: New York, the pile at Ground Zero
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She reaches the burning pile with Chuck Schumer the day after the towers fall, walks the perimeter in a borrowed hard hat, and goes back to Washington to get twenty billion dollars for the city out of a president who has just been handed a war. She takes a seat on the Armed Services Committee, the first New Yorker ever to hold one. She works the health effects of the dust on the responders for the rest of her time in office, long after the cameras go. New York, which called her a carpetbagger for two years, stops calling her one.
suggested_refs: The federal recovery appropriation for New York City, autumn 2001

stops.name: Washington, the Iraq authorization vote
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Senate vote of 11 October 2002; the quoted line is carried by Wikiquote only, dated to October 2002 without a day
stops.campa: The Senate takes up the authorization for the use of military force against Iraq and she votes yes, with twenty-eight other Democrats. Her floor speech runs long and hedges hard: she says the vote is not a vote for any doctrine of preemption, and that she casts it with conviction. It is the vote that costs her a nomination six years later, to a state senator from Illinois who was not in the chamber to cast one. She does not call it a mistake in public until 2014, in a book, twelve years after the fact.
stops.quote: This is probably the hardest decision I have ever had to make.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Senate floor remarks on the Iraq War authorization, October 2002, as carried by Wikiquote. The Congressional Record page S10288 returned HTTP 403 this session and the wording is unverified against the record
suggested_refs: The Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002, Senate roll call 237

stops.name: Baghdad, the Green Zone at Thanksgiving
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 2003 by CNN; the day is set to the Thanksgiving weekend of that year and is not separately fixed in the pool
stops.campa: Thirteen months after the vote she lands in Baghdad with Jack Reed and eats with the soldiers inside the walled district the Americans have made of Saddam Hussein's palaces. She tells them the country is behind them. She tells the reporters travelling with her that the reconstruction is not going the way Washington has been advertising it, and that the coalition needs help it is refusing to ask for. Both statements are recorded, and both will be read back to her from a podium in a Democratic primary five years on.
suggested_refs: The Republican Palace compound, later the US embassy, Baghdad

stops.name: Bagram, the other war
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 2003 by the Associated Press; the day follows the Baghdad leg of the same congressional trip and is not separately fixed
stops.campa: The same trip carries her north over the Hindu Kush to Bagram, the airfield the Soviets built and the Americans took in 2001 and did not leave. She spends the day with the troops there, in a war that nobody in Washington is arguing about, in the year the entire argument moved to Iraq. Afghanistan is still a war when she becomes Secretary of State, still a war when she leaves the department, and still a war on the night she loses the presidency thirteen years after this landing.
suggested_refs: Bagram Airfield, Parwan Province, Afghanistan

stops.name: Washington, the campaign suspended
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date. The pin is a Washington placeholder at the Capitol: the remarks were delivered at the National Building Museum, for which the pool supplies no coordinate
stops.campa: She has taken more primary votes than any losing candidate in the party's history, and on the seventh of June she stands in the great hall of the National Building Museum and endorses Barack Obama. Eighteen million people voted for her. She goes back to the Senate she never resigned, votes for his budget, campaigns for him through the autumn in states her voters hold. Six months later the man who beat her offers her the State Department, and she takes it.
stops.quote: Although we weren't able to shatter that highest, hardest glass ceiling this time, thanks to you, it's got about 18 million cracks in it.
stops.quote_source: Remarks suspending her presidential campaign, Washington, D.C., 7 June 2008. Wikiquote carries only the short clause 'It's got about 18 million cracks in it'; the fuller sentence given here is the widely reported form and was not checked against a primary transcript
suggested_refs: The Great Hall of the National Building Museum, 401 F Street NW, Washington

stops.name: Washington, the seventh floor of the Truman building
stops.date_confidence: attested for the swearing-in. The Chicago announcement narrated here is dated 1 December 2008: the Office of the Historian narrates the decision as November 2008, but no Chicago event occurred that month and the formal nomination went to the Senate on 20 January 2009
stops.campa: Obama announces her in Chicago, the city she was born in, four weeks after beating her, and the Senate confirms her ninety-four to two. She takes the seventh floor of the Truman building as the sixty-seventh Secretary of State and the third woman to hold the office. In four years she flies nine hundred and fifty-six thousand miles to a hundred and twelve countries, more than any secretary before her, and calls the doctrine smart power. She keeps her electronic mail on a private server in the basement at Chappaqua, and for six years almost nobody asks.
suggested_refs: The Harry S Truman Building, 2201 C Street NW, Washington
sources: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

stops.name: Islamabad, the questions taken in public
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 2009 by the New York Times; the day is set to the reported town hall sequence and is not separately fixed in the pool
stops.campa: She comes to Pakistan in a week when the drones are the only American subject anyone will discuss, and she does not stay behind the embassy wall. She takes the questions in the open: from students, from journalists, from tribal elders, on strikes her government will not officially admit exist. She tells a room of Pakistanis that it is hard to believe nobody in their government knows where al-Qaeda's leadership is, and could not reach them if they truly wanted to. Osama bin Laden is living in Abbottabad, a hundred kilometres north of the room.
suggested_refs: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Constitution Avenue, Islamabad

stops.name: Jerusalem, the inherited pin above the old city
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Repeated Jerusalem visits across 2009-2013 are documented in general terms and no date is fixed in the pool; September 2010 is chosen for the direct-talks round and is an inference, not an attestation
stops.campa: She comes to Jerusalem again and again across four years of shuttle diplomacy, to the settlements question and to the direct talks that open in September 2010 and close within a month over a construction freeze allowed to lapse. No single visit is dated precisely in the sources reached here. The city recurs on her schedule the way it recurs for every secretary of state before her, a fixed point on the shuttle-diplomacy circuit revisited under different governments and the same unresolved question each time.
suggested_refs: The September 2010 round of direct Israeli-Palestinian talks, suspended within a month
sources: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

stops.name: Paris, the recurring coordinate
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Paris is the atlas's most reused coordinate and her visits there as Secretary of State are real in general and unfixed in particular; September 2011 marks the Libya contact group period and is an inference, not an attestation
stops.campa: Paris is a city she passes through more than any other as secretary of state, the way every American secretary of state passes through it: the Libya contact group, the NATO ministerials, the Friends of Syria, the long lunches at the Quai d'Orsay where the French position is explained to her once more. No single visit stands out clearly in the record reached here. The pattern of returning again and again, on different business each time, is itself part of the nine hundred and fifty-six thousand miles she logs in four years.
suggested_refs: The Paris conference on Libya, 1 September 2011, and the Friends of Syria meetings
sources: atlas-canonical Paris coordinate, held across many traveler files
US Department of State travel records, 2009-2012

stops.name: Tripoli, the first cabinet officer after Gaddafi
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Two months after the capital falls she lands in Tripoli in an armoured convoy, the first American cabinet officer into post-Gaddafi Libya, and promises the transitional council another forty million dollars and help recovering the shoulder-fired missiles gone missing from the old regime's depots. Students mob her at the university. She was the voice inside the administration arguing for the intervention while the Pentagon argued against it, and this is the visit that certifies it as hers. Muammar Gaddafi is alive in Sirte, two days from the end.
suggested_refs: The National Transitional Council of Libya, Tripoli, October 2011
sources: US Department of State press pool reports, October 2011

stops.name: Sirte, the culvert and the sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from muammar_gaddafi.journey.json and marks his death site, not her location: she is in Kabul when the news reaches her
stops.campa: Muammar Gaddafi is dragged out of a drainage culvert on the western edge of Sirte, beaten, and shot, forty-two years after he took the country in a bloodless coup. She hears the news in Kabul from an aide holding out a telephone, with a CBS crew already recording her reaction, and she laughs before she has finished the sentence. The clip is cut loose from the rest of the interview and replayed against her for years afterward, through the entire campaign of 2016.
stops.quote: We came, we saw, he died.
stops.quote_source: Hillary Clinton, on camera to a CBS News crew on hearing of Gaddafi's death, 20 October 2011, as carried verbatim in muammar_gaddafi.journey.json
suggested_refs: The drainage culvert west of Sirte, Libya, 20 October 2011

stops.name: Yangon, the house on University Avenue
stops.date_confidence: attested; corrected from the geography lens on both counts. The lens coordinate fell 3.5 km southwest in central Yangon, and 1 December was the private dinner at the chief of mission's residence, not the meeting at the house
stops.campa: She drives out along Inya Lake to the compound at 54 University Avenue where Aung San Suu Kyi spent fifteen of twenty-one years under house arrest, the first American secretary of state in Burma since John Foster Dulles. The two women talk for two hours on the lakeside veranda and are photographed with their arms around each other, in white and in white. She has come with a proposition: sanctions traded for elections, in stages, each side moving only after the other has. The opening it starts will run for a decade and then fail.
suggested_refs: 54 University Avenue, Bahan Township, Yangon
sources: US Department of State press release, 1-2 December 2011

stops.name: Geneva, the Palais des Nations on Human Rights Day
stops.date_confidence: attested; quote wording corrected from the truncated form the quote lens carried, verified against multiple published books through Open Library full-text search
stops.campa: At the Palais des Nations, on International Human Rights Day, she tells the assembled diplomats of countries that jail men for whom they sleep with that being gay is not a Western invention, and that what is owed is not tolerance but law. Some delegations get up and leave the hall. The speech is built deliberately as the twin of the one she gave in Beijing sixteen years earlier, the identical grammatical move applied to a different excluded population, and she says so from the podium while she is making it.
stops.quote: Gay rights are human rights, and human rights are gay rights.
stops.quote_source: Remarks in Recognition of International Human Rights Day, Palais des Nations, Geneva, 6 December 2011. Full two-clause wording verified through Open Library full-text search of published books quoting the address; Wikiquote carries only the first clause
suggested_refs: The Palais des Nations, Geneva, and the December 2011 Human Rights Day address
sources: US Department of State speech transcript, 6 December 2011

stops.name: Cartagena, the Summit of the Americas
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summit dates of 14-15 April 2012; the attribution of the Secret Service scandal is corrected here, the agents belonged to the presidential detail and not to her staff
stops.campa: She attends the Summit of the Americas in the walled Caribbean city, thirty-three delegations arguing over Cuba's exclusion and over drug policy, and the summit is remembered for none of it. Secret Service agents of the presidential protective detail, in country ahead of the president, are found to have brought prostitutes to their hotel rooms, and eleven are removed. The story runs a month. A photograph of the secretary of state dancing at a Cartagena club runs alongside it, on the same pages, under the same dateline.
suggested_refs: Cartagena de Indias Convention Center, sixth Summit of the Americas, April 2012

stops.name: Beijing, the Great Hall of the People
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 2012 for the Beijing round of the Strategic and Economic Dialogue; coordinate corrected from a lens value that fell in Tiananmen Square. The lens's claim that February 2009 was an S&ED round is false: the first was July 2009 in Washington
stops.campa: She returns to Beijing for the Strategic and Economic Dialogue with a blind lawyer lying in an American hospital bed across the city. Chen Guangcheng had climbed his own wall, been driven to the embassy, left it, then changed his mind, and the negotiation over his exit runs underneath the formal one about currency and North Korea. He flies to New York nineteen days later. Seventeen years earlier she came to this city to say the sentence the government cut from the broadcast; the Great Hall receives her now as the ranking guest of the state.
suggested_refs: The fourth round of the US-China Strategic and Economic Dialogue, Beijing, May 2012
sources: US Department of State press releases, 2009-2012

stops.name: Benghazi, the compound in Western Fwayhat
stops.date_confidence: the attack is attested; this whole stop is tagged [R] in the source pool because the meaning of the episode is contested between official reports. Coordinate corrected from a Benghazi city centroid to the compound's district
stops.campa: A special mission compound in the Western Fwayhat district is attacked and burned, and Ambassador Chris Stevens and Sean Smith die there of smoke. Tyrone Woods and Glen Doherty are killed before dawn at the annex a mile away. It was never formally a consulate, whatever the coverage calls it. She is in Washington. The Accountability Review Board finds systemic security failures below her level; the House Select Committee, four years and eight inquiries later, finds no new evidence against her, and reports in the same summer she is nominated.
suggested_refs: The State Department Accountability Review Board report (2012) and the House Select Committee on Benghazi report (2016), read against each other
sources: House Select Committee on Benghazi Report (2016)

stops.name: Washington, the day of testimony
stops.date_confidence: the date is widely reported and the quote is tagged [R]: no hearing transcript was reachable this session, govinfo returned 404 and c-span returned 403, and the same exchange is also reported as House Oversight testimony that week
stops.campa: She testifies for five and a half hours before the Senate and the House on the same day, four months after taking public responsibility for the deaths. Senator Ron Johnson presses her on whether the attack began as a protest over a video, and she raises her voice to say that the men are dead and what matters now is finding whoever did it. The sentence is cut loose from its clause and printed alone, and it travels. Nine days later she leaves the department. In 2015 she sits eleven hours before a select committee and says it all again.
